words.shortDefinition: The rule that a variable's accessibility is determined by its position in the written source code, not by how or where functions are called at runtime.
words.simpleDefinition: Where a variable is visible is decided at write time, not at run time — by where it sits in the physical text of the source code. A function can always access names declared in any surrounding block where it was written, no matter how that function gets invoked later.
words.longDefinition: Lexical scope (also called static scope) means the scope chain for any given identifier is determined at parse time from the nesting structure of the source code. When the engine needs to resolve a name, it looks outward through each textually enclosing block until it finds a declaration, or reaches the global scope and throws a ReferenceError. This is in contrast to dynamic scope (used by some shell languages), where the call stack at runtime determines resolution. JavaScript, Python, Ruby, Go, and most modern languages are lexically scoped. Closures are a direct consequence of lexical scoping: a function captures its defining scope, not its calling scope, which is why `makeCounter()` works — the inner function closes over `count` from its lexical home.
words.connector: Think of lexical scope like addresses on a map — the street a building is on is printed on the map when the city is laid out; you don't redraw the map every time a delivery truck drives a different route.
words.techContext: Lexical scope is why closures work and why `this` in arrow functions is inherited from the surrounding code rather than re-bound on call. Misunderstanding it causes classic bugs like loop-variable capture with `var`.
words.exampleSentence: Because JavaScript uses lexical scope, the callback inside `setTimeout` could still access the `userName` variable declared in the outer function, even after that outer function had returned.
words.etymology: From Greek lexikon ('of words') — referring to the text of the source; 'scope' from Greek skopein ('to look at, observe').

words.shortDefinition: A function that can be stored in variables, passed as arguments, and returned from other functions, just like any data value.
words.simpleDefinition: When a language treats functions as values — meaning you can assign them to variables, pass them into other functions as arguments, and return them as results — those functions are called first-class. It is the property that makes callbacks, higher-order functions, and functional programming patterns possible.
words.longDefinition: A language supports first-class functions when functions carry no special restrictions compared to other values: they can be stored in variables and data structures, passed as arguments, returned from other functions, and even created anonymously at runtime (function expressions, arrow functions, lambdas). JavaScript, Python, Ruby, Go, Haskell, and most modern languages treat functions as first-class. Languages like older versions of C have function pointers — a limited approximation — but those are addresses, not true values. First-class functions enable higher-order functions (`map`, `filter`, `reduce`), callbacks and event handlers, closures, partial application, currying, and functional composition. The distinction matters because it separates languages where functions are merely syntax from those where they are genuine composable units of logic.
words.connector: Think of first-class functions like first-class airline tickets — the ticket holder (function) can go anywhere on the plane, sit anywhere, and be handed to someone else, just like any passenger (value).
words.techContext: Every time you pass a callback to `Array.prototype.map` or an event listener to `addEventListener`, you are exploiting first-class functions. React relies on them entirely — components are functions, event handlers are functions passed as props.
words.exampleSentence: Because JavaScript has first-class functions, we could store the validation logic in a configuration object and swap it out at runtime without changing the calling code.
words.etymology: The term 'first-class object' was coined by Christopher Strachey in the 1960s to describe values with no restrictions on their use.

words.shortDefinition: Implicit conversion of a value from one type to another by the language runtime.
words.simpleDefinition: When the language silently converts a value's type behind your back — `1 + '1'` becoming `'11'` in JavaScript, or `True + 1` becoming `2` in Python.
words.longDefinition: Coercion is the language doing 'helpful' type conversion you didn't ask for. It's the source of most weird bugs in dynamically typed languages: `[] == false` is true in JavaScript, `'5' < 6` works in Python 2 but raises in Python 3. Strict equality (`===`) and explicit conversion are the antidote.
words.techContext: TypeScript and Flow exist largely to eliminate accidental coercion. Linters flag `==` in favor of `===` for the same reason — coercion's edge cases are unlearnable.
words.exampleSentence: The bug was a coercion: `userId == 0` returned true for `''` because of JS's loose-equality rules.
words.etymology: From Latin coercere — to restrain, force together.
words.connector: Like an autocorrect that rewrites your message before sending — convenient when right, baffling when wrong.

codeExample.code:
// Coercion in the wild
1 + "1"      // "11"   (number coerced to string)
"5" - 1      // 4      (string coerced to number)
[] == false  // true   (both coerce to 0)
Null + 1     // ReferenceError, but null + 1 === 1

// Always prefer strict equality to avoid surprise:
0 == false   // true
0 === false  // false

words.shortDefinition: JavaScript's behavior of moving declarations to the top of their scope before code runs.
words.simpleDefinition: Variable and function declarations 'rise' to the top of their scope, so you can reference them before the line they appear on (with quirks).
words.longDefinition: JavaScript hoists `var` declarations and function declarations to the top of their scope. `var x` becomes accessible (as `undefined`) before its line; function declarations are fully callable. `let` and `const` are also hoisted but live in a 'temporal dead zone' — they exist but throw if referenced before their line.
words.techContext: Hoisting is the 'why' behind a class of confusing bugs: `console.log(x); var x = 5` prints `undefined`, not `ReferenceError`. Modern code uses `let`/`const` to opt into TDZ semantics, where the bug becomes a loud error.
words.exampleSentence: The bug was a hoisting trap: a `var` shadow inside the loop body silently reset the outer counter.
words.etymology: From the verb 'to hoist' — to lift up.
words.connector: Like declarations being yanked to the top of a function before any code runs — the engine reorders before executing.

words.shortDefinition: A technique where a function calls itself to solve progressively smaller instances of the same problem.
words.simpleDefinition: Programming technique where a function calls itself to solve smaller instances of the same problem — until reaching a simple base case. Powerful for traversing hierarchical data structures like trees or processing mathematical patterns.
words.longDefinition: Recursion requires a base case (trivially solved) and a recursive case (a smaller subproblem). Each call adds a frame to the call stack; without a base case the stack overflows. Tree traversal, divide-and-conquer, and parsing are naturally recursive.
words.connector: Think of recursion like Russian nesting dolls — you open one to find a smaller one inside, until you reach the tiny final doll.
words.techContext: Elegant for tree/graph problems but carries stack-depth risk. Iterative rewrites or tail-call optimisation are common remedies.
words.exampleSentence: We replaced the recursive directory traversal with an iterative version after hitting stack overflows on deeply nested paths.
words.etymology: from Latin recursio 'a running back', from recurrere 'to run back'.

codeExample.code:
def factorial(n: int) -> int:
    if n <= 1:              # base case
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)  # recursive case

words.shortDefinition: A function that retains access to variables from the scope in which it was defined, even after that scope has closed.
words.simpleDefinition: A function that remembers and retains access to its parent scope's variables — even after that parent scope has finished executing. Essential for data encapsulation, event handling, and maintaining state in functional programming patterns.
words.longDefinition: Closures bundle a function with its surrounding lexical environment. They enable data encapsulation, callbacks with state, and partial application. In JavaScript, closures are the mechanism behind module patterns and many React hooks.
words.connector: Think of a closure like a lunchbox you packed at home — when you open it later at work, everything you put in is still there.
words.techContext: Essential for event handlers, async callbacks, and factory functions. Stale closures capturing outdated state are a common React bug.
words.exampleSentence: The counter keeps its own private count thanks to a closure — no global variable needed.
words.etymology: from Latin clausura 'a closing'; applied to programming by Peter Landin (1964) in SECD machine theory.

words.shortDefinition: Unchangeable after creation — modifications produce a new value rather than altering the original.
words.simpleDefinition: Object or data structure that cannot be modified after its creation — where any 'change' results in the creation of a brand new instance. Improves predictability and safety, especially in concurrent and functional programming environments.
words.longDefinition: Immutability prevents accidental modification and makes reasoning about code easier. Immutable data structures enable safe concurrency, time-travel debugging, and pure functions. Strings, tuples, and frozen objects are typically immutable.
words.connector: Think of immutable like a printed book — once finished, you cannot edit the pages; you must print a second edition.
words.techContext: Immutability is central to functional programming and React state management. It eliminates entire classes of bugs.
words.exampleSentence: We switched to immutable data structures so concurrent updates couldn't corrupt shared state.
words.etymology: from Latin immutabilis 'unchangeable' from in- ("not") + mutare ("to change").

words.shortDefinition: A function passed as an argument to be invoked later, often after an asynchronous operation completes.
words.simpleDefinition: Function passed as an argument to be executed later, typically once a long-running or asynchronous task completes. Enables non-blocking code flow by allowing systems to notify the original caller when results are ready.
words.longDefinition: Callbacks enable asynchronous programming and event-driven architectures. They decouple the caller from the called, allowing frameworks to control execution flow. Deeply nested callbacks create 'callback hell', addressed by promises and async/await.
words.connector: Think of a callback like leaving your number with a restaurant — they will call you back when your table is finally ready.
words.techContext: Ubiquitous in JavaScript, Node.js, and event systems. Understanding callback timing and scope is critical for async code.
words.exampleSentence: We refactored the nested callbacks into async/await to escape callback hell and improve readability.
words.etymology: call from Old Norse kalla 'to cry out'; back from Old English bæc — literally 'call back'; computing use from early event systems.

words.shortDefinition: An object representing the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation.
words.simpleDefinition: Object representing the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation — acting as a placeholder for a future value. Simplifies async logic by replacing nested callbacks with a cleaner, chainable syntax.
words.longDefinition: Promises provide a cleaner alternative to callbacks for async code. A promise starts pending, then settles to either fulfilled (with a value) or rejected (with an error). Chaining via .then() and .catch() flattens callback pyramids.
words.connector: Think of a promise like an online order confirmation — you don't have the package yet, but you have a guarantee it is coming.
words.techContext: Core to modern JavaScript. Promises underpin async/await, fetch(), and most async APIs in Node and browsers.
words.exampleSentence: Switching from callbacks to promises made our error handling consistent and eliminated callback hell.
words.etymology: from Latin promissum 'a pledge'; computing use from E (1980s) and standardized in JavaScript ES6 (2015).

words.shortDefinition: Non-blocking execution where operations complete in the background without halting the program.
words.simpleDefinition: Programming pattern allowing long-running tasks to execute in the background without blocking the main execution thread. Essential for maintaining responsive user interfaces and high-performance server-side applications handling many simultaneous requests.
words.longDefinition: Asynchronous programming allows long-running tasks (I/O, network, timers) to execute without blocking the main thread. Control returns immediately; results arrive later via callbacks, promises, or async/await. Essential for responsive UIs and scalable servers.
words.connector: Think of async like starting the laundry — you don't wait for the machine to finish; you do other work until it beeps.
words.techContext: Async is the default in Node.js and JavaScript. Understanding the event loop, microtasks, and macrotasks is critical.
words.exampleSentence: The UI froze because we ran the database query synchronously instead of making it async.
words.etymology: from Greek asynchronos 'not happening at the same time' from a- ("not") + syn- ("together") + chronos ("time").

words.shortDefinition: A set of rules that assigns types to program elements and enforces constraints on their usage.
words.simpleDefinition: Set of logical rules assigning categories — like number, string, or boolean — to variables and functions to ensure safe usage. Prevents common bugs by checking that data operations are valid before the code runs.
words.longDefinition: Type systems prevent certain classes of errors by ensuring operations are valid for the data types involved. Static type systems check types at compile time; dynamic systems check at runtime. Strong vs. weak typing governs implicit conversions.
words.connector: Think of a type system like labeled recycling bins — they ensure bottles only go with bottles, catching mix-ups early.
words.techContext: Type systems range from JavaScript's dynamic weak typing to Rust's static strong typing. TypeScript adds static types to JavaScript.
words.exampleSentence: Switching to TypeScript caught dozens of type errors at compile time that would have crashed in production.
words.etymology: type from Greek typos 'impression, figure'; system from Greek systema 'organized whole'.

words.shortDefinition: A contract defining methods or properties that implementing types must provide.
words.simpleDefinition: Formal contract defining expected methods and properties without prescribing implementation details — allowing disparate code modules to interact predictably. Promotes loose coupling and simplifies testing by enabling easy swapping of components.
words.longDefinition: Interfaces specify what an object can do without dictating how it does it. They enable polymorphism, dependency injection, and loose coupling. A class or type can implement multiple interfaces, supporting flexible design.
words.connector: Think of an interface like a driver's license — it proves you can drive any car, regardless of the brand or engine type.
words.techContext: Central to languages like Java, TypeScript, and Go. Interfaces enable testability via mocking and decoupling via abstraction.
words.exampleSentence: We defined a PaymentGateway interface so we could swap Stripe for PayPal without changing business logic.
words.etymology: from Latin inter 'between' + facies 'face' — literally 'surface between'; computing use from 1960s.

words.shortDefinition: A variable that stores the memory address of another value rather than the value itself.
words.simpleDefinition: Variable storing the direct memory address of another value rather than the data itself — serving as a reference. Pointers enable efficient memory manipulation and complex data structures but require careful management to avoid crashes.
words.longDefinition: Pointers enable direct memory manipulation, dynamic data structures (linked lists, trees), and efficient parameter passing. Misused pointers cause segmentation faults, dangling references, and memory leaks. Higher-level languages replace pointers with references.
words.connector: Think of a pointer like a library reference number — it is not the book itself, but tells you exactly which shelf to find it on.
words.techContext: Fundamental in C and C++. Understanding pointers clarifies references in Java, Python, and JavaScript.
words.exampleSentence: The crash was caused by a null pointer dereference — we accessed memory that had already been freed.
words.etymology: from point (to indicate) + -er; computing use from early assembly and C programming.

codeExample.code:
int x = 42;
int *ptr = &x;     // ptr stores address of x
printf("%d", *ptr); // dereference → 42

*ptr = 100;        // modifies x through pointer
printf("%d", x);    // 100

words.shortDefinition: Automated memory management identifying and reclaiming memory occupied by unreachable or unused objects.
words.simpleDefinition: The automatic background process of identifying and reclaiming memory occupied by objects no longer reachable by the program. It prevents memory leaks by ensuring unused resources are freed — without requiring manual developer intervention.
words.longDefinition: Garbage Collection is an automated memory management process that identifies objects no longer reachable from the root of the application and reclaims their memory. Modern engines typically use a 'Mark-and-Sweep' algorithm: the collector 'marks' reachable objects and 'sweeps' away everything else. While efficient, GC cycles can cause 'stop-the-world' pauses that result in dropped frames. Developers can minimize these pauses by reducing object churn and avoiding memory leaks, such as those caused by forgotten event listeners.
words.connector: Think of garbage collection like a hotel cleaning crew — they enter rooms only after guests have checked out to prepare the space for someone new.
words.techContext: While automatic, developers can cause memory leaks by accidentally keeping references to large objects (e.g., in global variables or forgotten intervals).
words.exampleSentence: Frequent garbage collection pauses were causing our animation to stutter, so we reduced object allocation in our render loop.
words.etymology: Metaphor for cleaning up 'trash' (unused memory).

codeExample.code:
let user = { name: "John" };
user = null; // The object previously referenced by 'user' is now eligible for garbage collection.

words.shortDefinition: A data structure that maps keys to values using a hash function for O(1) average-case lookup.
words.simpleDefinition: Efficient data structure mapping unique keys to specific values using a hash function — providing near-instant lookup performance. Ideal for caching, counting, and indexing, where quick retrieval from large datasets is required.
words.longDefinition: Hash maps (also called hash tables, dictionaries, or associative arrays) store key-value pairs. A hash function converts keys to array indices. Collisions are resolved via chaining or open addressing. They power JavaScript objects, Python dicts, and database indexing.
words.connector: Think of a hash map like a hotel key-card system — you provide the room number and instantly find the correct door.
words.techContext: Fundamental for caching, counting, indexing, and deduplication. Understanding hash collisions and load factors optimizes performance.
words.exampleSentence: We used a hash map to track user sessions in memory for O(1) lookup by session ID.
words.etymology: hash from Middle English hacchen 'to chop'; map from Latin mappa 'napkin, cloth' — a visual representation.

codeExample.code:
counts = {}          # hash map
counts['apple'] = 5
counts['banana'] = 3

print(counts['apple'])  # O(1) lookup → 5

words.shortDefinition: A last-in-first-out data structure where elements are added and removed from the same end.
words.simpleDefinition: Ordered data structure following Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) principles — where items are added and removed from the same end. Essential for managing function calls, undo histories, and certain search algorithms.
words.longDefinition: Stacks support push (add to top) and pop (remove from top) in O(1) time. They model function call stacks, undo mechanisms, and depth-first traversal. Stack overflow occurs when the call stack exceeds its size limit.
words.connector: Think of a stack like a pile of plates in a cafeteria — the last one placed on top is the first one taken.
words.techContext: Understanding the call stack is critical for debugging recursion, async behavior, and stack traces. Also used in parsers and calculators.
words.exampleSentence: The recursive function caused a stack overflow because it never hit the base case and exhausted the call stack.
words.etymology: from Old Norse stakkr 'haystack'; computing use from early descriptions of memory allocation (1940s).

codeExample.code:
stack = []
stack.append(1)    # push
stack.append(2)
stack.append(3)

print(stack.pop())  # 3 — LIFO
print(stack.pop())  # 2

words.shortDefinition: Syntax that unpacks values from arrays or properties from objects into distinct variables in a single statement.
words.simpleDefinition: A concise syntax — introduced in ES2015 — for pulling specific values out of arrays or objects and binding them to named variables in one expression, rather than accessing each property or index individually.
words.longDefinition: Destructuring assignment lets you extract multiple values from data structures in a single readable line. Object destructuring pulls named properties: `const { a, b } = obj` is equivalent to `const a = obj.a; const b = obj.b`. Array destructuring unpacks by position: `const [first, second] = arr`. Both support default values (`const { x = 0 } = {}`), renaming (`const { longName: short } = obj`), rest collection (`const { a, ...rest } = obj`), and nested patterns. Function parameters can also be destructured: `function greet({ name, age }) {}` extracts directly from the passed object. Destructuring is purely syntactic sugar — it generates the same property-access code under the hood — but it eliminates repetition and signals intent clearly, especially when pulling many fields out of API responses or React props.
words.connector: Think of destructuring like unpacking a suitcase — instead of reaching in one item at a time, you lay everything out in labeled piles in a single motion.
words.techContext: Ubiquitous in modern JS/TS: `const { data, error, loading } = useQuery(...)` in React, `const [state, setState] = useState(...)`, and parameter destructuring in route handlers. Pairs naturally with the spread/rest operator.
words.exampleSentence: Destructuring the API response into `{ user, token, expiresAt }` made the code far more readable than three separate property accesses.
words.etymology: From Latin de- ('apart') + structura ('arrangement'); coined in programming to describe 'taking apart' a structured value.

words.shortDefinition: An operator that returns its right-hand operand only when the left-hand side is null or undefined, not for any falsy value.
words.simpleDefinition: The `??` operator returns the right side only when the left side is `null` or `undefined` — unlike `||`, which also triggers on `0`, `''`, and `false`. This lets you provide a default value while still treating zero, empty strings, and false as intentional values.
words.longDefinition: Nullish coalescing (`??`) was introduced in ES2020 to fill a long-standing gap. Before it, developers used `||` for defaults: `const x = input || 'default'`. But `||` treats any falsy value as 'missing', so `0 || 42` gives `42` — wrong when zero is a valid input. `??` narrows the condition to only `null` or `undefined`, which are the language's explicit 'nothing here' sentinels. The optional chaining operator (`?.`) pairs naturally with `??`: `user?.address?.city ?? 'Unknown'` safely traverses the chain and falls back only on actual absence. TypeScript models this at the type level: `??` narrows away `null | undefined` from the type of the left operand. An assignment variant `??=` was added in ES2021: `obj.cache ??= computeExpensiveValue()` initializes the property only if it has never been set.
words.connector: Think of `??` like a strict understudy policy — the understudy goes on only if the lead is completely absent (`null`/`undefined`), not just nervous (falsy like `0` or `''`).
words.techContext: Prefer `??` over `||` for default values whenever zero, empty string, or false are meaningful. Use `??=` for lazy initialization of cache fields. Combine with `?.` for safe deep-property access with fallback.
words.exampleSentence: Switching the user-count default from `count || 0` to `count ?? 0` fixed the display bug where a legitimate zero-count was being replaced by the fallback.
words.etymology: Latin nullus ('none') + -ish (adjectival suffix); 'coalescing' from Latin coalescere ('to grow together, merge').

words.shortDefinition: A string delimited by backticks that allows embedded expressions and multi-line text without concatenation.
words.simpleDefinition: A string type introduced in ES2015, wrapped in backticks (`` ` ``), that allows you to embed any JavaScript expression directly inside `${...}` placeholders and to write strings that span multiple lines without escape characters.
words.longDefinition: Template literals replace the brittle string-concatenation pattern (`'Hello, ' + name + '\!'`) with a clean interpolation syntax: `` `Hello, ${name}\!` ``. Any valid JavaScript expression can appear inside `${...}` — function calls, ternary operators, arithmetic, even nested template literals. Multi-line strings are written naturally; the newlines in the source become newlines in the string. A more advanced form — 'tagged templates' — allows a function to preprocess the raw pieces and interpolated values, enabling powerful DSLs: SQL query builders, CSS-in-JS libraries (styled-components), localization engines, and HTML sanitizers all use tagged templates to intercept and process interpolation at call time.
words.connector: Think of template literals like a form letter with fill-in-the-blank fields — you write the text once with placeholders, and the values snap in at runtime.
words.techContext: Standard in modern JS/TS for constructing URLs, log messages, HTML snippets, and SQL fragments. Tagged template literals power styled-components' `css` tag, GraphQL's `gql` tag, and many testing assertion libraries.
words.exampleSentence: Rewriting the URL builder with template literals eliminated five levels of concatenation and made the query string structure immediately readable.
words.etymology: From Latin templum ('pattern, frame') + literalis ('of letters'); 'literal' in programming means a fixed value in source code.

words.shortDefinition: The linked series of objects JavaScript traverses to resolve a property or method that is not found directly on a given object.
words.simpleDefinition: Every JavaScript object has a hidden reference (its prototype) to another object. When you access a property, JavaScript first checks the object itself, then walks up through each linked prototype until it finds the property or hits `null`. This chain is how method inheritance works without classical classes.
words.longDefinition: JavaScript's inheritance model is prototype-based rather than class-based. Every object has an internal `[[Prototype]]` slot (accessible as `__proto__` or via `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)`) pointing to another object. When the engine looks up a property, it searches the object itself first; if not found, it follows the `[[Prototype]]` link and searches there, repeating until the chain ends at `null` (the prototype of `Object.prototype`). This traversal is the prototype chain. ES2015 `class` syntax is syntactic sugar over this mechanism: `class Dog extends Animal` sets up the prototype chain so that `Dog.prototype.[[Prototype]] === Animal.prototype`. Method resolution order, `instanceof` checks, and `Object.create()` all operate on the prototype chain. Mutations to a prototype object — like adding a method to `Array.prototype` — affect every instance already in memory, which is why extending built-in prototypes ('monkey-patching') is discouraged.
words.connector: Think of the prototype chain like a family tree for property lookup — if you don't have a skill yourself, you check if your parent does, then your grandparent, until someone in the family can do it or the search ends.
words.techContext: Understanding the prototype chain explains why `obj.hasOwnProperty('x')` differs from `'x' in obj`: the first checks only the object itself, the second walks the chain. It also explains how `Array.prototype.map` is shared by every array without being stored on each one.
words.exampleSentence: The `toString()` call worked even though we never defined it, because the prototype chain led up to `Object.prototype.toString` before returning undefined.
words.etymology: Greek prototypon ('first impression, original') + 'chain' from Old French chaîne (linked series).

words.shortDefinition: A regular JavaScript function called with `new` to create and initialize a new object instance.
words.simpleDefinition: A plain function designed to be called with the `new` keyword. When called that way, JavaScript automatically creates a fresh empty object, sets `this` to it inside the function, links the new object's prototype to the function's `.prototype` property, and returns the object — so the function just fills in properties with `this.x = value`.
words.longDefinition: Before ES2015 classes, constructor functions were the idiomatic way to define object blueprints in JavaScript. By convention they start with a capital letter (e.g., `function Person(name) {}`). When invoked with `new`, four things happen: (1) a new empty object is created; (2) its `[[Prototype]]` is set to `ConstructorFn.prototype`; (3) `this` inside the function body refers to that new object; (4) if the function does not explicitly return an object, the new object is returned automatically. Methods shared by all instances should be placed on `Constructor.prototype`, not inside the function body, to avoid duplicating them per instance. ES2015 `class` syntax desugars directly to this pattern; `class Dog {}` is essentially a constructor function with cleaner syntax, mandatory `new`, and nicer `super` handling. Understanding constructor functions is essential for reading pre-ES2015 codebases, React class component internals, and low-level prototype manipulation.
words.connector: Think of a constructor function like a cookie cutter — each call with `new` stamps out a new cookie (object) using the same shape (prototype), but each cookie is its own independent piece of dough.
words.techContext: In modern code you'll usually write `class` syntax, but the underlying mechanism is a constructor function. React class components, Node.js EventEmitter, and much browser-native API inherit from constructor function patterns. Watch for the `new` omission bug — calling a constructor without `new` makes `this` the global object.
words.exampleSentence: The bug was traced to calling the `Queue` constructor function without `new` — `this.items` was being set on the global object instead of the intended instance.
words.etymology: Latin constructor ('one who puts together') + 'function' from Latin functio ('performance, execution').

words.shortDefinition: Transforming a function of N arguments into a chain of N single-argument functions.
words.simpleDefinition: Instead of `f(a, b, c)`, you call `f(a)(b)(c)` — each call returns a new function awaiting the next argument.
words.longDefinition: Currying lets you partially apply a function — fix the first argument and pass the resulting specialized function around. Common in functional codebases (Ramda, Haskell, OCaml) for building composable pipelines: `multiply(2)` becomes a "double" function, `filter(isEven)` becomes a reusable "evens-only filter".
words.techContext: JavaScript libraries like Ramda and Lodash/fp curry by default. React-Redux's `connect(mapState)(mapDispatch)(Component)` is canonical curried API. Idiomatic in TypeScript when generic constraints get long.
words.exampleSentence: Curry the API client so each module gets a pre-configured request function with the auth header baked in.
words.etymology: Named after logician Haskell Curry — though Moses Schönfinkel discovered it first.
words.connector: Like a vending machine that takes coins one at a time — it's not 'broken' between coins, it's just waiting for the next one.

words.shortDefinition: The study of how an algorithm's resource consumption — time or memory — scales as its input grows.
words.simpleDefinition: A measure of how much harder an algorithm works — in terms of time steps or memory used — as you feed it larger inputs. Understanding it lets you predict which solution will hold up at scale and which will grind to a halt when data doubles.
words.longDefinition: Algorithmic complexity is the formal study of an algorithm's resource requirements as a function of input size n. Time complexity counts the number of operations performed; space complexity counts the memory footprint. Both are expressed using asymptotic notation — most commonly Big O — which describes the dominant growth term as n approaches infinity, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms. Common complexity classes, in ascending cost: O(1) constant, O(log n) logarithmic (binary search), O(n) linear (single pass), O(n log n) linearithmic (efficient sorting), O(n²) quadratic (naive nested loops), O(2ⁿ) exponential (recursive subset enumeration). Analysing complexity involves identifying the algorithm's dominant operation — comparisons, swaps, recursive calls — and counting how many times it executes relative to input size. Complexity theory extends this into worst, average, and best cases; amortized analysis; and NP-hardness.
words.connector: Think of algorithmic complexity like comparing shipping strategies: ground shipping may be fine for one box (O(1) flat rate), but air freight that costs proportionally more per kilogram (O(n)) or one that needs every pair of boxes weighed against each other (O(n²)) becomes painfully apparent at scale.
words.techContext: Knowing the complexity class of your solution informs whether it will survive production. Swapping an O(n²) solution with an O(n log n) one typically becomes critical when n reaches tens of thousands. Interview candidates are routinely asked to state the time and space complexity of their solutions.
words.exampleSentence: Profiling showed that the report generator had O(n²) complexity because it was checking every transaction against every other one — switching to a hash-map lookup brought it to O(n).
words.etymology: Arabic al-Khwarizmi (the scholar whose name became 'algorithm') + Latin complexus ('entwined, complicated').

words.shortDefinition: When an inner-scope declaration of a name hides — shadows — an identically named variable in an enclosing outer scope.
words.simpleDefinition: When you declare a variable inside a block or function that has the same name as one in an outer scope, the inner declaration 'shadows' the outer one. Code inside that inner scope sees only the inner variable; the outer one still exists but is temporarily invisible.
words.longDefinition: Variable shadowing occurs whenever the same identifier is declared in two nested scopes. Within the inner scope, the inner declaration takes precedence for all name lookups; the outer variable is neither modified nor deleted, it is simply unreachable by that name from inside the inner scope. Shadowing is legal in virtually all block-scoped languages (JavaScript with `let`/`const`, Python, Go, Java, Swift) and is sometimes intentional — for example, shadowing `err` in successive Go `if err \!= nil` blocks. However, unintentional shadowing is a frequent source of subtle bugs: a developer adds a local variable with a common name (`count`, `i`, `data`) and accidentally stops reading or writing the outer one. Linters like ESLint's `no-shadow` rule and Go's shadow analyzer detect these cases. Shadowing differs from variable mutation (which changes the outer value) and from a fresh block-scoped redeclaration with `let` in the same scope (which is a SyntaxError).
words.connector: Think of variable shadowing like standing in front of a painting — the painting (outer variable) still exists on the wall behind you, but everyone in the room looking from inside that spot sees only you (inner variable) instead.
words.techContext: Go developers often shadow `err` deliberately in short `if` blocks. JavaScript's `no-shadow` ESLint rule catches accidental shadows. In closures, a shadowed loop variable is the classic reason to prefer `let` over `var` — `let` creates a new binding per iteration, `var` shares one binding across all iterations.
words.exampleSentence: The loop counter never advanced because a new `i` declared with `var` inside the callback shadowed the outer `i`, but only within the callback — a classic shadowing trap.
words.etymology: Old English sceadwian ('to cast a shadow'); 'variable' from Latin variabilis ('changeable').

words.shortDefinition: The automatic bubbling of an uncaught error up through the call stack until a matching handler is found or the process terminates.
words.simpleDefinition: When a function throws an error it cannot handle itself, the error automatically travels up to the calling function, then to its caller, and so on up the call stack until a `try/catch` block intercepts it. If nothing catches it, the runtime terminates the program or, in a browser, logs an unhandled rejection.
words.longDefinition: Exception propagation is the runtime mechanism that unwinds the call stack when an error is thrown and no handler exists in the current frame. In synchronous code, the exception climbs the call stack frame by frame until it reaches a `try/catch` block whose `catch` clause matches the error type, or until the stack is exhausted and the runtime receives an uncaught exception. In JavaScript's async/await model, a rejected promise propagates along the promise chain: an `await` without a surrounding `try/catch` re-throws into the calling async function, which itself becomes a rejected promise. Every async function in the chain must either handle the error or implicitly propagate it further. Understanding propagation is crucial for designing error boundaries — in React (component error boundaries), Express (error middleware), or Go (explicit error returns up every call layer). Thoughtful propagation means catching at the right level: too low (every small function) produces noise; too high (only at the process boundary) loses context.
words.connector: Think of exception propagation like a hot potato — if you catch it you handle it; if you don't, you toss it to the person behind you, and it keeps traveling until someone grabs it or it falls off the end of the table.
words.techContext: In Node.js, unhandled promise rejections trigger the `unhandledRejection` process event and, in newer versions, crash the process. In React, exceptions propagating out of the render tree are caught by the nearest `ErrorBoundary` component. Go intentionally has no propagation — every error must be explicitly checked and returned.
words.exampleSentence: The outer `try/catch` in the request handler intercepted the database exception that propagated up through three layers of async service calls, allowing us to return a structured 500 response.
words.etymology: Latin exceptio ('a taking out') + propagatio ('spreading, extending').
